title: Redwood Optimize walkthrough - batching & KV cache (Meridian Payments)

Customer requested security docs and a pilot to validate latency under their peak patterns.

Cost model: tokens saved vs additional compute
Dedicated vs Hosted routing and fallbacks
Next steps: pilot + security docs + benchmark run

meeting_header:
Date: 2027-03-22 | Time: 15:00 - 15:55 UTC | Duration: 55m
Attendees: Claire Park (Redwood AE), Devon Li (Redwood SE), Avery Chen (Redwood Solutions); Samir Rao (Meridian), Lena Ortiz (Meridian), Marcus Nguyen (Meridian), Priya Desai (Meridian)
transcript:
[00:00] Claire Park: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. Quick intros - im Claire, AE at Redwood. Devon is our SE who will run the Optimize walkthrough.
[00:18] Devon Li: Hey all, yeah thanks. Today we wanna focus on batching and caching recommendations, prefix and KV cache, and a simple cost model so you can see token save math. If at any point stop me and ask questions.
[00:35] Samir Rao: Sounds good. Quick context - we run payments APIs, 60ms median p99 300ms during peak, and want to keep latency under 250ms p99. We also want to reduce token spend for conversational assistant.
[00:50] Devon Li: Totally. Two high-level levers: batching, which increases throughput by combining requests into GPU micro-batches, and prefix/KV cache which avoids re-evaluating long context prefixes.
[01:10] Lena Ortiz: When you say prefix cache can you explain difference between prefix and KV cache? I sometimes see those used interchangeably.
[01:20] Devon Li: Good question. Prefix cache is simpler - we cache decoder prefix outputs for repeated beginnings of sequences; KV cache is more general fast lookup of past key/value states so you can resume generation without redoing the prefix. In practice we call it KV cache when resuming long conversations or multi-turn flows.
[01:40] Marcus Nguyen: Does that mean we need sticky routing to keep KV cache hit rate high?
[01:48] Devon Li: Not necessarily sticky forever, but you get higher hit rates if routing favors same worker for a user session. We can do session-aware routing or keep a small hot pool. Tradeoff is cost vs latency.
[02:05] Claire Park: For Meridian, from what you described, I'd recommend starting with a hybrid: hosted with a dedicated hot pool for low-latency sessions and fallback to hosted variants for lower priority or bursty traffic.
[02:20] Priya Desai: Security question - we need KMS integration and audit logs, also SOC2. Do you have docs?
[02:28] Claire Park: Yep, we published SOC2 and KMS integration guides. I ll share links after the call.
[02:36] Devon Li: Back to batching - there are two knobs: target batch size and max latency window. For conversational flows with short responses, smaller batch sizes (16-64 tokens) but tighter windows to keep latency; for embeddings or async jobs bigger batches are fine.
[02:55] Devon Li: Example: on an A100-class worker, with continuous batching, raising effective batch from 4->16 improves tokens/sec by ~2.5x but increases median latency by ~20ms in our benchmarks.
[03:15] Samir Rao: That 20ms is acceptable if our p99 stays under 250, but how does that affect model choice?
[03:23] Devon Li: Good point - quantized model variants reduce memory and inference cost, but can add slight quality regression for open-domain generation. We generally recommend 8-bit quantization for latency-sensitive workloads where quality tolerances are higher. We can run an eval set against your prompts.
[03:45] Marcus Nguyen: I'd like to see the evals. Also what are hit-rate expectations for KV cache in a payments chatbot? A lot of prompts share the same account-level prefixes.
[03:56] Devon Li: If your flows reuse account-specific prefix text (like account metadata and instructions), we often see KV hit rates 40-60% for well-structured flows. For free-text chat it s lower. That maps directly into tokens saved: 40% hit means you avoid re-evaluating 40% of prefix tokens on average.
[04:18] Devon Li: On the cost model: we build a simple per-100k-requests model. Token cost = (avg_prompt_tokens + avg_generation_tokens - saved_tokens_from_cache) * cost_per_token. Compute cost changes with batch efficiency.
[04:35] Devon Li: Quick worked example: avg prompt 120 tokens, generation 60 tokens, prefix accounts for 80 tokens. With 50% KV hit we save 40 tokens per request. At 100k reqs, that s 4M tokens saved. At our hosted price thats roughly $X (Devon: see deck), and you re also getting better GPU utilization.
[05:00] Marcus Nguyen: Could you step through the spreadsheet?
[05:05] Devon Li: Sure I ll paste the link to the benchmark spreadsheet and the Optimize deck in chat. Note: link is redwood.com/decks/optimize-batch-cache.pdf and redwood.com/benchmarks/meridian-sample.
[05:22] Lena Ortiz: I noticed in earlier calls you mentioned continuous batching and micro-batching. Can you explain the difference?
[05:30] Devon Li: Micro-batching is grouping requests within a single GPU step; continuous batching is letting the runtime keep a small buffer and flush based on latency window so throughput increases without big latency spikes.
[05:45] Samir Rao: Do we need to tune per-route? Our payments endpoints vary widely - some routes are quick threshold queries, others are long generative receipts.
[05:59] Claire Park: Yes, per-route policies are best practice. Redwood Console supports per-route batching windows and cache policies so you can set conservative values for high-SLO routes and aggressive batching for low-SLO ones.
[06:15] Priya Desai: On compliance again - is persisted KV cache encrypted and can it be disabled?
[06:22] Devon Li: Persisted caches are encrypted at rest, and you can disable persistence and rely on in-memory caches only. We also support customer-managed KMS in Private deployments.
[06:35] Marcus Nguyen: What about cold-starts and cache warming? If we have a pilot, how do we avoid poor latency on day 1?
[06:45] Devon Li: For pilots we recommend seeding the cache with common prefixes and running a short warm-up traffic replay. We can script that from the traffic sample you provide.
[06:55] Claire Park: Ok, let's go deeper into hit-rate math and latency tradeoffs. If you accept slightly higher median latency, you can increase batch windows to get more batching efficiency; that reduces per-token compute cost. But if you bump it too high you risk p99s.
[07:15] Devon Li: Also routing policies matter: session-affinity to keep KV hits high, a small warm-hot dedicated pool for important customers, and fallbacks to open-hosted models if dedicated capacity is saturated.
[07:33] Samir Rao: Can you quantify cost savings vs Dedicated reserved capacity? We re evaluating a dedicated commit for predictable throughput.
[07:42] Claire Park: Dedicated will lower unit compute cost and give you predictable throughput. Combined with caching you get multiplicative savings: lower per-token compute + fewer tokens evaluated. We can model a 20-40% reduction versus pure hosted depending on your commit size and cache hit rate.
[08:02] Marcus Nguyen: Sounds promising. For the pilot we'd want to validate p99 at peak concurrency of ~1.2k requests/min.
[08:12] Devon Li: Noted. Please include that in the traffic sample. We'll run the pilot on a dedicated hot pool sized to approximate that concurrency and measure p99, throughput, and cache hit rates.
[08:25] Lena Ortiz: For the SLOs, we also need tracing and token-level cost breakdowns per route. Is that available?
[08:31] Claire Park: Yes, Redwood Console provides per-route token and cost breakdown, and tracing hooks to map requests to logs. We'll share screenshots in the deck.
[08:40] Devon Li: Small aside - sometimes company names and acronyms are transcribed wrong in these notes; e g we might see K V as K dash V in auto transcripts, ignore these small glitches.
[08:52] Samir Rao: ha noted. Can you talk about tail-latency mitigation?
[08:58] Devon Li: Sure - two quick items: one, keep a small dedicated hot pool so high-SLO traffic avoids noisy neighbors; two, implement preemption windows and priority queuing so critical requests jump the queue. Also consider model cascade: fast smaller model for quick answers, bigger model for fallback.
[09:18] Marcus Nguyen: On model cascade - how does caching interplay? If we cache prefix from small model responses is that useful when we later call the bigger model?
[09:28] Devon Li: The cache is per model family variant; cross-model cache hits are rare. We recommend using the same model family for cached prefixes if you plan to cascade.
[09:38] Claire Park: We're about halfway through, want to pause for any deep technical questions before we run through the cost spreadsheet?
[09:45] Marcus Nguyen: No deep blockers, go ahead.
[09:50] Devon Li: Ok spreadsheet walkthrough: Column A is route, B is avg prompt tokens, C avg gen tokens, D prefix tokens, E expected KV hit, F saved tokens per req = D * E, G net tokens per req = A+B+ C - F, H token cost per million, I compute cost adj from batching. Then total monthly cost.
[10:15] Devon Li: For Meridian sample we used route 'account-summary' with avg prompt 140, gen 50, prefix 90, assumed 45% KV hit, gives saved 40.5 tokens per req and total token reduction ~22%.
[10:30] Lena Ortiz: If we increase KV hit to 60% via session affinity, what's the diminishing returns?
[10:36] Devon Li: Diminishing returns appear as you approach full hit on very small prefixes; also more affinity can increase routing overhead. Typically biggest wins are first 30-50% of hit rate.
[10:50] Samir Rao: Any gotchas for PCI-sensitive data in cache?
[10:56] Devon Li: Don't persist raw PCI in cache. Trim or token-munge before caching; we can help define sanitizer rules. Persisted caches also can be configured to exclude sensitive fields.
[11:10] Marcus Nguyen: Can we set per-route cache TTLs?
[11:13] Devon Li: Yes, per-route TTL and per-user slice controls.
[11:20] Claire Park: Ok I'm going to call out the concrete pilot scope: 2-week pilot, dedicated hot pool sized for 1.2k rpm, seed KV cache with common prefixes, run traffic replay, measure p99 and hit rates, then review and tune. Approve?
[11:36] Lena Ortiz: Looks good, need to get legal and security sign-off but team ok.
[11:42] Priya Desai: We'll need a data processing addendum and SOC2 artifacts.
[11:47] Claire Park: We'll attach those to the follow-up email.
[11:52] Devon Li: One more note on measurement: measure end-to-end latency including network hop; sometimes improvements at token compute level don't fully reflect user-observed p99.
[12:05] Samir Rao: Understood.
[12:08] Claire Park: Ok closing the technical part. Quick recap of next steps and action items - I ll send pricing, SOW, the deck and benchmark spreadsheet. Claire to schedule pilot kickoff.
[12:25] Devon Li: Thanks everyone. We'll follow up on the links: redwood.com/decks/optimize-batch-cache.pdf and redwood.com/benchmarks/meridian-sample.
[12:33] Lena Ortiz: Thanks, bye.
[12:35] Meeting ended
